exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Mean of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: A bolt manufacturer determines that $1.5\%$ of the bolts produced are defective. A quality control inspection will check $200$ randomly selected bolts. What is the mean number of defective bolts in the sample?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of defective bolts in the sample.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=200$ bolts

  • the probability of selecting a defective bolt is $p=1.5\%=0.015$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(200,0.015).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the mean is given by \[ \textrm E[X] = np, \] where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the mean number of defective bolts is \[ \begin{align*} \textrm E[X] &= np \\[3pt] &= (200)(0.015) \\[3pt] &= 3. \end{align*} \]

example.title: Finding the Mean of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: A student answers a true-false test choosing each answer at random. If the test has $17$ questions, what is the mean of the number of correct answers?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of correct answers.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=17$ questions

  • the probability of selecting the correct answer in each question is \[ p=\dfrac{1}{2}. \]

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B\left(17,\dfrac12\right).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the mean is given by \[ \textrm E[X] = np, \] where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the mean number of correct answers is \[ \begin{align*} \textrm E[X] &= np \\[3pt] &= 17 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \\[3pt] &= 8.5. \end{align*} \]

question.text: A coin is biased so that the probability of it landing on heads is $0.7.$ The coin is tossed $15$ times. What is the mean number of times the coin lands on heads?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times the coin lands on heads.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=15$ tosses

  • the probability of landing on heads for each toss is $p=0.7$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(15,0.7).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the mean is given by \[ \textrm E[X] = np, \] where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the mean of the number of times the coin lands on heads is

\[ \begin{align*} \textrm E[X] &= np \\[3pt] &= (15)(0.7) \\[3pt] &= 10.5. \end{align*} \]

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Variance of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: The probability that a product of a company is defective is $0.04.$ Random samples of $50$ products are taken from the week's production. What is the variance of the number of defective products in the sample?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of defective products.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=50$ products in the sample

  • the probability that a product is defective is $p=0.04$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(50,0.04).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by \[ \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p), \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of defective products is

\[ \begin{align*} \textrm{Var}[X] &= np(1-p) \\[3pt] &= (50)(0.04)(1-0.04) \\[3pt] &= (50)(0.04)(0.96) \\[3pt] &= 1.92. \end{align*} \]

question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of groups that do not arrive.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=30$ reservations

  • the probability that a group doesn't arrive is $p=15\%=0.15$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(30,0.15).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by \[ \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p), \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of groups that do not arrive is

\[ \begin{align*} \textrm{Var}[X] &= np(1-p) \\[3pt] &= (30)(0.15)(1-0.15) \\[3pt] &= (30)(0.15)(0.85) \\[3pt] &= 3.825. \end{align*} \]

question.text: A coffee shop has determined that $35\%$ of its customers buy a piece of cake when visiting. A random sample of $40$ customers is taken. What is the variance in the number of customers that bought a piece of cake?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of clients that bought a piece of cake.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=40$ customers

  • the probability of a customer buying a piece of cake is $p=35\%=0.35$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(40,0.35).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by \[ \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p), \] where $n$ is the number of experiments, and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of clients that bought a piece of cake is

\[ \begin{align*} \textrm{Var}[X] &= np(1-p) \\[3pt] &= (40)(0.35)(1-0.35) \\[3pt] &= (14)(0.65) \\[3pt] &= 9.1. \end{align*} \]

example.title: Finding the Variance of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: Three doors in a computer game hide an apple, and a fourth door hides an orange. Fifteen players are playing the game, and each player is asked to choose one door at random. What is the variance of the number of players winning an apple?
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of players winning an apple.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=15$ players in the game

  • the probability of choosing a door that hides an apple is $p=\dfrac34$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B\left(15,\dfrac34\right).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by \[ \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p), \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of players winning an apple is \[ \begin{align*} \textrm{Var}[X] &= np(1-p) \\[5pt] &= 15 \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \left( 1 - \dfrac{3}{4} \right) \\[5pt] &= 15 \cdot \dfrac{3}{4} \cdot \dfrac 14\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{45}{16}. \end{align*} \]

example.title: Finding the Variance of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: A fair six-sided die is rolled $12$ times. What is the variance of the number of times we get a number less than $3?$
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of time we get a number less than $3.$

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=12$ rolls

  • the probability of getting a number less than $3$ (i.e., a $1$ or $2$) on any roll of the die is \[ p=\dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{3}. \]

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B\left(12,\dfrac13\right).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the variance is given by \[ \textrm{Var}[X] = np(1-p), \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the variance of the number of times we get a number less than $3$ is \[ \begin{align*} \textrm{Var}[X] &= np(1-p) \\[5pt] &= 12 \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{3} \right) \\[5pt] &= 4 \cdot \dfrac{2}{3} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8}{3}. \end{align*} \]

exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Standard Deviation of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: Approximately $20\%$ of the emails received in an account are spam. If there are $20$ inbox emails, what is the standard deviation of the number of spam emails received? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of spam emails.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=20$ inbox emails

  • the probability of being a spam email is $p=20\%=0.20$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(20,0.20).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by \[ \textrm{SD}[X] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]}= \sqrt{np(1-p)} \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of spam emails received is

\[ \begin{align*} \textrm{SD}[X] &= \sqrt{np(1-p)} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{(20)(0.20)(1-0.20)} \\[3pt] &= \sqrt{3.2} \\[3pt] &= 1.789 \end{align*} \]

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

example.title: Finding the Standard Deviation of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: A fair twelve-sided die with sides labeled with numbers $1$ through $12$ is rolled $80$ times. What is the standard deviation of the number of times we get a number divisible by $5?$
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of times we get a number divisible by $5.$

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=80$ rolls

  • the probability of getting a number divisible by $5$ (i.e., a $5$ or a $10$) on any roll of the die is \[ p=\dfrac{2}{12}=\dfrac 16. \]

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B\left(80,\dfrac16\right).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by \[ \textrm{SD}[X] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)}, \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of times we get a number divisible by $5$ is \[ \begin{align*} \textrm{SD}[X] &= \sqrt{np(1-p)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{80 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} \cdot \left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{6} \right)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{80 \cdot \dfrac{1}{6} \cdot \dfrac{5}{6}} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{\dfrac{100}{9}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {10}{3}. \end{align*} \]

example.title: Finding the Standard Deviation of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: A student answers a multiple-choice test choosing each answer at random. If the test has $16$ questions, and each question has $4$ possible answers with only one correct answer, what is the standard deviation of the number of correct answers? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of correct answers.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=16$ questions

  • the probability of selecting the correct answer in each question is \[ p=\dfrac{1}{4}. \]

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B\left(16,\dfrac14\right).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by \[ \textrm{SD}[X] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)}, \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of correct answers is \[ \begin{align*} \textrm{SD}[X] &= \sqrt{np(1-p)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{16 \cdot \dfrac{1}{4} \cdot \left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{4} \right)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{3} \\[5pt] &= 1.732 \end{align*} \] rounded to $3$ decimal places.

example.title: Finding the Standard Deviation of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: A basketball player has a $70\%$ success rate in shooting from the free throw line during a season. The player has ten shots from the free throw line in one match. What is the standard deviation of the number of successful free throws? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be the number of successful free throws.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=10$ shots from the free throw line in the match

  • the probability that the player is successful from the free throw line is $p=70\%=0.7$

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B(10,0.7).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by \[ \textrm{SD}[X] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)}, \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of successful free throws is \[ \begin{align*} \textrm{SD}[X] &= \sqrt{np(1-p)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{(10)(0.7)(1-0.7)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{(10)(0.7)(0.3)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{2.1} \\[5pt] &\approx 1.449 \end{align*} \] rounded to $3$ decimal places.

example.title: Finding the Standard Deviation of a Binomial Random Variable

question.text: A fair six-sided die is rolled $10$ times. What is the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
question.explanation:
Let the random variable $X$ be equal to the number of times we get an even number.

Here, we have the following information:

  • there are $n=10$ rolls of the die

  • the probability of getting an even number (i.e., a $2,$ $4,$ or $6$) on any roll of the die is \[ p=\dfrac{3}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}. \]

So, $X$ follows a binomial distribution, where $X\sim B\left(10,\dfrac12\right).$

For a binomial random variable $X,$ the standard deviation is given by \[ \textrm{SD}[X] = \sqrt{\textrm{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{np(1-p)}, \] where $n$ is the number of experiments and $p$ is the probability of success on each experiment.

So, the standard deviation of the number of times we get an even number is \[ \begin{align*} \textrm{SD}[X] &= \sqrt{np(1-p)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{10 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot \left( 1 - \dfrac{1}{2} \right)} \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{2.5} \\[5pt] &= 1.581 \end{align*} \] rounded to $3$ decimal places.
